2.Damascus Gate
The grandest of the Old City's gates, its twin towers and machicolations rebuilt in 1537 over a Roman triumphal gate raised by Emperor Hadrian — the only gate to keep its Arabic name, Bab al-Amud, since at least the 10th century.

Lina · Hummus Ben Sira
Sabich

Food Delivery
Wolt
Foreign number: accepted. — sign-up takes a foreign mobile number and the verification code arrives by SMS from an international sender.
The dominant delivery app in Jerusalem, covering the Mamilla and city-center restaurant scene in full; payment is by foreign Visa or Mastercard with no local ID required, though card-issuer foreign-transaction fees may apply.
wolt.com
10bis
Foreign number: not accepted. — sign-up asks for an Israeli Teudat Zehut national ID to link a card, which a foreign visitor does not have.
Israel's other major food-ordering platform, strong on workplace lunch delivery, but its account setup is built around local ID and a local card — tourists consistently report being unable to complete checkout.
10bis.co.il

Getting Around
Gett
Foreign number: not accepted. — registration requires an Israeli mobile number for SMS verification; a foreign SIM does not receive the code.
Israel's most widely used taxi-hailing app, with strong Jerusalem coverage and English-language support; visitors typically register once they have a local eSIM or SIM active.
gett.com
Yango
Foreign number: accepted. — sign-up takes an international mobile number and the SMS verification code arrives from a foreign-reachable sender.
A licensed-taxi-hailing app with growing coverage in Jerusalem; shows an upfront fixed price before booking and accepts cash as well as card, though its driver density is thinner than Gett's outside the city center.
yango.com
Jerusalem Light Rail
A single 23-stop line running from Mount Herzl through the city center to Pisgat Ze'ev, passing the Old City walls near Damascus Gate.
Jerusalem has a tram system — operated by Cfir. Line used on this trip: the Red Line.
cfir.co.il

Day Trips by Train
Tel Aviv · 30 min
Israel's coastal commercial capital, a direct 30 - 40 minute train — beaches, the White City's Bauhaus architecture, and the Carmel Market, a full contrast to Jerusalem's historic core.
book at: Israel Railways or Omio
Haifa · 1 hr 40 min
A port city built up Mount Carmel, best known for the golden-domed Baháʼí Gardens terracing down to the harbor; reached via a change of train at Tel Aviv onto the coastal line north.
book at: Israel Railways or Omio
Akko · 2 hr
A UNESCO-listed Ottoman and Crusader walled port town north of Haifa, its underground Crusader halls and covered market reached by continuing north on the coastal line past Haifa.
book at: Israel Railways or Omio
Worth Knowing

A city where the same building serves more than one faith

Mount Zion holds the clearest example: David's Tomb, the Room of the Last Supper and Dormition Abbey sit stacked in and around one small complex, sacred to Judaism, Christianity and, historically, Islam at once. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre is shared among six Christian denominations under one roof, each holding a fixed portion of the building down to the minute of who may clean which step — a 19th-century arrangement called the Status Quo that still governs the church today.

Most ticketed national sites and government offices close on Saturday for Shabbat, and many shift to shortened Friday hours from early afternoon — this affects Yad Vashem, City of David, Mount Herzl and the Chagall Windows at Hadassah, all of which this itinerary places on non-Friday, non-Saturday visiting days by design. The Western Wall and its plaza are the exception and stay open around the clock, busiest and most atmospheric as Shabbat begins on Friday evening.

Modest dress — shoulders and knees covered — is expected at the Western Wall, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, David's Tomb and the Dome of the Rock plaza; men are asked to cover their heads at the Wall and at David's Tomb, and paper kippahs are provided free at both.
